claim: The 4.4 million-year-old hominin partial skeleton is attributed to Ardipithecus ramidus.
source: The 4.4 million-year-old hominin partial skeleton attributed to Ardipithecus ramidus preserves a foot that purportedly shares morphometric affinities with monkeys, but this interpretation remains controversial.
evidence: The age and taxonomic attribution are stated directly in the abstract.

claim: The foot of Ardipithecus ramidus was previously interpreted to share morphometric affinities with monkeys.
source: The 4.4 million-year-old hominin partial skeleton attributed to Ardipithecus ramidus preserves a foot that purportedly shares morphometric affinities with monkeys, but this interpretation remains controversial.
evidence: The abstract references a prior interpretation that is being challenged.

claim: The interpretation of the Ardipithecus ramidus foot as monkey-like remains controversial.
source: The 4.4 million-year-old hominin partial skeleton attributed to Ardipithecus ramidus preserves a foot that purportedly shares morphometric affinities with monkeys, but this interpretation remains controversial.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the controversy.

claim: The foot of Ardipithecus ramidus is most similar to living chimpanzee and gorilla species among a large sample of anthropoid primates.
source: Here I show that the foot of Ar. ramidus is most similar to living chimpanzee and gorilla species among a large sample of anthropoid primates.
evidence: This is the primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by the PCA and cluster analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The foot morphology of Ardipithecus ramidus suggests that the evolutionary precursor of hominin bipedalism was African ape-like terrestrial quadrupedalism and climbing.
source: The foot morphology of Ar. ramidus suggests that the evolutionary precursor of hominin bipedalism was African ape-like terrestrial quadrupedalism and climbing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the morphometric similarity to African apes and evolutionary modeling.

claim: The elongation of the midfoot in Ardipithecus ramidus relative to the African apes is consistent with hypotheses of increased propulsive capabilities associated with an early form of bipedalism.
source: The elongation of the midfoot and phalangeal reduction in Ar. ramidus relative to the African apes is consistent with hypotheses of increased propulsive capabilities associated with an early form of bipedalism.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative measurements and biomechanical reasoning.

claim: Phalangeal reduction in Ardipithecus ramidus relative to the African apes is consistent with hypotheses of increased propulsive capabilities associated with an early form of bipedalism.
source: The elongation of the midfoot and phalangeal reduction in Ar. ramidus relative to the African apes is consistent with hypotheses of increased propulsive capabilities associated with an early form of bipedalism.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative measurements and biomechanical reasoning.

claim: The modern human foot was derived from an ancestral form adapted to terrestrial plantigrade quadrupedalism.
source: This study provides evidence that the modern human foot was derived from an ancestral form adapted to terrestrial plantigrade quadrupedalism.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on ancestral state estimation and evolutionary modeling.

claim: Terrestrial bipedalism is widely regarded as a shared-derived characteristic of the hominin clade.
source: Terrestrial bipedalism is widely regarded as a shared-derived characteristic of the hominin clade and understanding its evolution is one of the central foci of biological anthropology (Darwin, 1871; Wasburn, 1967; Fleagle et al., 1981; Richmond et al., 2001; Gebo, 1996; Begun, 2004; Lovejoy et al., 2009a; White et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Understanding the evolution of bipedalism is one of the central foci of biological anthropology.
source: Terrestrial bipedalism is widely regarded as a shared-derived characteristic of the hominin clade and understanding its evolution is one of the central foci of biological anthropology (Darwin, 1871; Wasburn, 1967; Fleagle et al., 1981; Richmond et al., 2001; Gebo, 1996; Begun, 2004; Lovejoy et al., 2009a; White et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Adaptive explanations for the origin of bipedalism are inherently difficult to test directly.
source: There are numerous adaptive explanations for the origin of bipedalism (Darwin, 1871; Hewes, 1961; Lovejoy, 1981; Rose, 1991; Washburn, 1960; Hunt, 1996) that are inherently difficult to test directly (Smith and Wood, 2017), but each of them depends on alternative hypothetical models for the morphology and locomotor behavior of the human-chimpanzee last common ancestor (LCA; Richmond et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a methodological observation supported by citation.

claim: Each adaptive explanation for the origin of bipedalism depends on alternative hypothetical models for the morphology and locomotor behavior of the human-chimpanzee last common ancestor.
source: There are numerous adaptive explanations for the origin of bipedalism (Darwin, 1871; Hewes, 1961; Lovejoy, 1981; Rose, 1991; Washburn, 1960; Hunt, 1996) that are inherently difficult to test directly (Smith and Wood, 2017), but each of them depends on alternative hypothetical models for the morphology and locomotor behavior of the human-chimpanzee last common ancestor (LCA; Richmond et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between adaptive hypotheses and ancestral reconstructions.

claim: The partial skeleton of Ardipithecus ramidus purportedly lacks postcranial specializations associated with hominoid-like orthogrady, vertical climbing, and suspension.
source: The partial skeleton of the early hominin Ardipithecus ramidus purportedly lacks postcranial specializations associated with hominoid-like orthogrady, vertical climbing, and suspension (Lovejoy et al., 2009a; Lovejoy et al., 2009b; Lovejoy et al., 2009c; White et al., 2009; White et al., 2015), which challenges conventional understandings of ape and human ancestry (Darwin, 1871; Keith, 1923; Morton, 1922; Wasburn, 1967; Gebo, 1992; Gebo, 1996; Williams, 2012).
evidence: This is a claim from prior literature being discussed.

claim: The interpretation of Ardipithecus ramidus as lacking hominoid-like postcranial specializations challenges conventional understandings of ape and human ancestry.
source: The partial skeleton of the early hominin Ardipithecus ramidus purportedly lacks postcranial specializations associated with hominoid-like orthogrady, vertical climbing, and suspension (Lovejoy et al., 2009a; Lovejoy et al., 2009b; Lovejoy et al., 2009c; White et al., 2009; White et al., 2015), which challenges conventional understandings of ape and human ancestry (Darwin, 1871; Keith, 1923; Morton, 1922; Wasburn, 1967; Gebo, 1992; Gebo, 1996; Williams, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of prior interpretations.

claim: The foot of Ardipithecus ramidus was argued to possess monkey-like midfoot stabilizing and propulsive morphologies that were inferred to be primitive for great apes.
source: In particular, the foot of Ar. ramidus was argued to possess monkey-like midfoot stabilizing and propulsive morphologies that were inferred to be primitive for great apes (Lovejoy et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is a claim from prior literature being discussed.

claim: Lovejoy and colleagues suggested that the Ardipithecus ramidus foot was consistent with 'above branch plantigrady' and a form of locomotion termed 'arboreal multigrady'.
source: Lovejoy and colleagues (Lovejoy et al., 2009a; White et al., 2015) suggested that the Ar. ramidus foot was consistent with 'above branch plantigrady' and a form of locomotion termed 'arboreal multigrady' (White et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a claim from prior literature being discussed.

claim: The African apes are viewed as 'adaptive cul-de-sacs' by Lovejoy and colleagues.
source: The African apes are viewed as 'adaptive cul-de-sacs' (Lovejoy et al., 2009b: pg. 104) that independently evolved adaptations for vertical climbing given the purported lack of 'the peculiar substrate-conforming, hand-like grasping foot of living African apes' (White et al., 2015: pg. 4883) in Ar. ramidus and in White and colleagues' reconstruction of the Homo-Pan LCA.
evidence: This is a claim from prior literature being discussed.

claim: Foot proportions are hypothesized to reflect variation in locomotor behavior among anthropoid primates.
source: Foot proportions (e.g., tarsal, metatarsal, and phalangeal lengths) are hypothesized to reflect variation in locomotor behavior among anthropoid primates (Midlo, 1934; Schultz, 1963a; Schultz, 1963b; Jolly, 1967; Strasser, 1992; Strasser, 1994).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature.

claim: The modern human foot has been highly modified in response to the biomechanical constraints of terrestrial bipedalism.
source: Furthermore, the modern human foot has been highly modified in response to the biomechanical constraints of terrestrial bipedalism (Morton, 1922; Gebo, 1992; Harcourt-Smith and Aiello, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The first three principal components account for 96% of the total variance in the sample.
source: The first three principal components account for 96% of the total variance in the sample and clearly separate taxonomic groups along previously hypothesized axes of morphological variation (Schultz, 1963a; Schultz, 1963b; Jolly, 1967; Strasser, 1992; Strasser, 1994).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the PCA analysis.

claim: The first three principal components clearly separate taxonomic groups along previously hypothesized axes of morphological variation.
source: The first three principal components account for 96% of the total variance in the sample and clearly separate taxonomic groups along previously hypothesized axes of morphological variation (Schultz, 1963a; Schultz, 1963b; Jolly, 1967; Strasser, 1992; Strasser, 1994).
evidence: This is a result from the PCA analysis that confirms prior hypotheses.

claim: The first principal component accounts for 63% of the variance.
source: The first principal component accounts for 63% of the variance and is positively loaded by the lengths of the fifth metatarsal and fourth proximal phalanx.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the PCA analysis.

claim: The first principal component is positively loaded by the lengths of the fifth metatarsal and fourth proximal phalanx.
source: The first principal component accounts for 63% of the variance and is positively loaded by the lengths of the fifth metatarsal and fourth proximal phalanx.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the PCA analysis.

claim: The second principal component accounts for 18% of the variance.
source: The second principal component accounts for 18% of the variance and is positively loaded by the lengths of the first metatarsal and fourth proximal phalanx, and negatively loaded by the length of the fifth metatarsal.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the PCA analysis.

claim: The second principal component is positively loaded by the lengths of the first metatarsal and fourth proximal phalanx, and negatively loaded by the length of the fifth metatarsal.
source: The second principal component accounts for 18% of the variance and is positively loaded by the lengths of the first metatarsal and fourth proximal phalanx, and negatively loaded by the length of the fifth metatarsal.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the PCA analysis.

claim: The third principal component represents 15% of the variance.
source: The third principal component, which represents 15% of the variance, is positively loaded by the length of the first metatarsal (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the PCA analysis.

claim: The third principal component is positively loaded by the length of the first metatarsal.
source: The third principal component, which represents 15% of the variance, is positively loaded by the length of the first metatarsal (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the PCA analysis.

claim: The distribution of anthropoid taxa in the PCA is consistent with predictions based on locomotor behavior.
source: The distribution of anthropoid taxa in the PCA is consistent with predictions based on locomotor behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PCA results in relation to locomotor behavior.

claim: More terrestrial taxa fall at the negative end of PC1 with shorter metatarsals and phalanges.
source: For example, the more terrestrial taxa fall at the negative end (Homo, Pan, Gorilla, Theropithecus, Papio, and Erythrocebus) with shorter metatarsals and phalanges, whereas the most arboreal, suspensory, taxa fall at the positive end of PC1 (e.g., Pongo and Ateles).
evidence: This is an observation from the PCA plot (Figure 2) and the underlying data.

claim: The most arboreal, suspensory taxa fall at the positive end of PC1.
source: For example, the more terrestrial taxa fall at the negative end (Homo, Pan, Gorilla, Theropithecus, Papio, and Erythrocebus) with shorter metatarsals and phalanges, whereas the most arboreal, suspensory, taxa fall at the positive end of PC1 (e.g., Pongo and Ateles).
evidence: This is an observation from the PCA plot (Figure 2) and the underlying data.

claim: A UPGMA cluster analysis shows that of the 44 extant taxa presented, Ardipithecus ramidus is most similar to Pan and Gorilla.
source: A UPGMA cluster analysis (cophenetic correlation coefficient = 0.82) shows that of the 44 extant taxa presented here Ar. ramidus is most similar to Pan and Gorilla (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the cluster analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cophenetic correlation coefficient for the UPGMA cluster analysis is 0.82.
source: A UPGMA cluster analysis (cophenetic correlation coefficient = 0.82) shows that of the 44 extant taxa presented here Ar. ramidus is most similar to Pan and Gorilla (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical measure of the cluster analysis quality.

claim: Ardipithecus ramidus possesses a cuboid that is only slightly elongated relative to African apes.
source: Univariate comparisons show that Ar. ramidus possesses a cuboid that is only slightly elongated relative to African apes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), a relatively short fourth proximal phalanx (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), and an intrinsically elongated first metatarsal like African apes and atelids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a comparative observation from univariate analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Ardipithecus ramidus possesses a relatively short fourth proximal phalanx.
source: Univariate comparisons show that Ar. ramidus possesses a cuboid that is only slightly elongated relative to African apes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), a relatively short fourth proximal phalanx (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), and an intrinsically elongated first metatarsal like African apes and atelids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a comparative observation from univariate analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Ardipithecus ramidus possesses an intrinsically elongated first metatarsal like African apes and atelids.
source: Univariate comparisons show that Ar. ramidus possesses a cuboid that is only slightly elongated relative to African apes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), a relatively short fourth proximal phalanx (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), and an intrinsically elongated first metatarsal like African apes and atelids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a comparative observation from univariate analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: All variables scale with slight negative allometry in that larger species tend to have relatively shorter metatarsals, phalanges, and tarsals.
source: All variables scale with slight negative allometry in that larger species tend to have relatively shorter metatarsals, phalanges, and tarsals.
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic generalized least squares regression analysis.

claim: The length of the talar trochlea scales isometrically with body mass.
source: The only exception is the length of the talar trochlea, which scales isometrically with body mass.
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic generalized least squares regression analysis.

claim: The PC scores used in the evolutionary analyses are not correlated with body mass.
source: The PC scores used in the evolutionary analyses are not correlated with body mass (pGLS p = 0.08 or higher), which suggests that body mass is not responsible for driving the differences in intrinsic foot proportions among anthropoid groups.
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic generalized least squares regression analysis.

claim: Body mass is not responsible for driving the differences in intrinsic foot proportions among anthropoid groups.
source: The PC scores used in the evolutionary analyses are not correlated with body mass (pGLS p = 0.08 or higher), which suggests that body mass is not responsible for driving the differences in intrinsic foot proportions among anthropoid groups.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of correlation between PC scores and body mass.

claim: Model comparisons using multiple criteria show that the multi-optima OU models are a better fit to the data than a Brownian or single-optimum OU model.
source: Model comparisons using multiple criteria (AIC, AICc, SIC) show that the multi-optima OU models are a better fit to the data than a Brownian or single-optimum OU model (Supplementary file 2), which suggests there are multiple adaptive peaks associated with foot proportions among anthropoid primates.
evidence: This is a result from the evolutionary modeling analysis.

claim: There are multiple adaptive peaks associated with foot proportions among anthropoid primates.
source: Model comparisons using multiple criteria (AIC, AICc, SIC) show that the multi-optima OU models are a better fit to the data than a Brownian or single-optimum OU model (Supplementary file 2), which suggests there are multiple adaptive peaks associated with foot proportions among anthropoid primates.
evidence: This is an inference from the evolutionary modeling results.

claim: Simulations show that there is adequate power to distinguish between alternative evolutionary models.
source: Simulations show that there is adequate power to distinguish between alternative models and provides support for the a priori model selection results obtained using AICc (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is a result from the simulation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The multivariate evolutionary modeling analyses confirm that among anthropoid primates intrinsic foot proportions are linked to locomotor behavior.
source: The multivariate evolutionary modeling analyses presented here confirms that among anthropoid primates intrinsic foot proportions are linked to locomotor behavior (Midlo, 1934; Schultz, 1963a; Schultz, 1963b; Jolly, 1967; Strasser, 1992; Strasser, 1994).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the evolutionary modeling analysis that confirms prior hypotheses.

claim: The combination of evolutionary modeling with ancestral estimations provides evidence for homoplasy in the evolution of anthropoid foot proportions.
source: The combination of evolutionary modeling with ancestral estimations provides evidence for homoplasy in the evolution of anthropoid foot proportions, which strengthens hypotheses about the link between morphology and behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the combined evolutionary modeling and ancestral state estimation analyses.

claim: Erythrocebus probably evolved a terrestrially adapted, digitigrade foot characterized by short phalanges, a short hallux, and long non-hallucal metatarsals independently of Theropithecus and Papio.
source: For example, Erythrocebus probably evolved a terrestrially adapted, digitigrade foot characterized by short phalanges, a short hallux, and long non-hallucal metatarsals independently of Theropithecus and Papio.
evidence: This is an inference about convergent evolution from the evolutionary modeling results.

claim: African apes and Ardipithecus ramidus occupy a distinct phenotypic optimum characterized by short phalanges, short metatarsals, moderately elongated tarsals, and a long hallux.
source: African apes and Ar. ramidus occupy a distinct phenotypic optimum characterized by short phalanges, short metatarsals, moderately elongated tarsals, and a long hallux.
evidence: This is a result from the evolutionary modeling analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The more terrestrial hominines and cercopithecines probably evolved short phalanges in parallel.
source: Although the more terrestrial hominines (Homo, Ardipithecus, Pan, Gorilla) and cercopithecines (Papio, Theropithecus, Erythrocebus) probably evolved short phalanges in parallel (Figures 1 and 2), the hominines retain an intrinsically elongated hallux and short non-hallucal metatarsals while the terrestrial cercopithecines display the opposite configuration (Schultz, 1963a; Schultz, 1963b).
evidence: This is an inference about convergent evolution from the data and evolutionary modeling.

claim: Hominines retain an intrinsically elongated hallux and short non-hallucal metatarsals while the terrestrial cercopithecines display the opposite configuration.
source: Although the more terrestrial hominines (Homo, Ardipithecus, Pan, Gorilla) and cercopithecines (Papio, Theropithecus, Erythrocebus) probably evolved short phalanges in parallel (Figures 1 and 2), the hominines retain an intrinsically elongated hallux and short non-hallucal metatarsals while the terrestrial cercopithecines display the opposite configuration (Schultz, 1963a; Schultz, 1963b).
evidence: This is a comparative observation from the data.

claim: The difference in foot proportions between terrestrially adapted apes and monkeys are similar to the differences between plantigrade and digitigrade carnivorans.
source: The difference in foot proportions between terrestrially adapted apes and monkeys are similar to the differences between plantigrade and digitigrade carnivorans (Taylor, 1976).
evidence: This is a comparative analogy supported by citation.

claim: The unique combination of traits in the hominine foot supports the hypothesis that such feet are adapted to both terrestrial heel-strike plantigrade quadrupedalism and vertical climbing.
source: The unique combination of these traits in the hominine foot supports the hypothesis that such feet are adapted to both terrestrial heel-strike plantigrade (rather than digitigrade) quadrupedalism and vertical climbing, which is consistent with previous suggestions based on comparative anatomy and behavioral observations (Fleagle et al., 1981; Gebo, 1996; Prost, 1980; Gebo, 1992; DeSilva, 2009; Prang, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from the morphometric data that is consistent with prior hypotheses.

claim: If Ardipithecus ramidus and the Homo-Pan LCA were adapted to more generalized quadrupedalism and climbing as originally suggested, then the Ardipithecus ramidus foot skeleton should not have been placed in the same selective regime as the African apes.
source: If Ar. ramidus and the Homo-Pan LCA were adapted to more generalized quadrupedalism and climbing as originally suggested (Lovejoy et al., 2009a; White et al., 2009) or 'arboreal multigrady' as later revised (White et al., 2015); see also Fernández et al., 2018), then the Ar. ramidus foot skeleton should not have been placed in the same selective regime as the African apes (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the evolutionary modeling results that contradicts prior interpretations.

claim: The ancestral estimations provide support for the hypothesis that modern humans evolved from an ancestor with African ape-like foot proportions.
source: The ancestral estimations provide support for the hypothesis that modern humans evolved from an ancestor with African ape-like foot proportions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the ancestral state estimation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Modern humans have the longest cuboids of any of the anthropoid primates sampled in this study.
source: Modern humans have the longest cuboids of any of the anthropoid primates sampled here (Figure 2), which reflects a biomechanical strategy for lengthening the foot's load arm to enhance aspects of propulsion (i.e., range of motion) while simultaneously restricting metatarsal length to minimize bending moments associated with plantigrady (Lovejoy et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The long cuboid in modern humans reflects a biomechanical strategy for lengthening the foot's load arm to enhance aspects of propulsion while simultaneously restricting metatarsal length to minimize bending moments associated with plantigrady.
source: Modern humans have the longest cuboids of any of the anthropoid primates sampled here (Figure 2), which reflects a biomechanical strategy for lengthening the foot's load arm to enhance aspects of propulsion (i.e., range of motion) while simultaneously restricting metatarsal length to minimize bending moments associated with plantigrady (Lovejoy et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is a biomechanical interpretation supported by citation.

claim: The cuboid elongation of Ardipithecus ramidus from the estimated LCA is more modest than previously reported.
source: Although the cuboid elongation of Ar. ramidus from the estimated LCA is more modest than previously reported (Lovejoy et al., 2009a), it is more parsimoniously interpreted to be derived in the direction of modern humans from an African ape-like ancestor with a short midfoot, rather than an ancestral retention from a more monkey-like great ape ancestor (Lovejoy et al., 2009a; Lovejoy et al., 2009b; White et al., 2015; McNutt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparative observation that contradicts prior claims.

claim: The cuboid elongation in Ardipithecus ramidus is more parsimoniously interpreted to be derived in the direction of modern humans from an African ape-like ancestor with a short midfoot, rather than an ancestral retention from a more monkey-like great ape ancestor.
source: Although the cuboid elongation of Ar. ramidus from the estimated LCA is more modest than previously reported (Lovejoy et al., 2009a), it is more parsimoniously interpreted to be derived in the direction of modern humans from an African ape-like ancestor with a short midfoot, rather than an ancestral retention from a more monkey-like great ape ancestor (Lovejoy et al., 2009a; Lovejoy et al., 2009b; White et al., 2015; McNutt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference from the ancestral state estimation that contradicts prior interpretations.

claim: Midfoot elongation is consistent with the functional hypothesis of increased propulsive capabilities associated with the form of bipedalism practiced by Ardipithecus ramidus.
source: Midfoot elongation is consistent with the functional hypothesis of increased propulsive capabilities associated with the form of bipedalism practiced by Ar. ramidus (Lovejoy et al., 2009a; White et al., 2015; Suwa et al., 2009; Kimbel et al., 2014; Kozma et al., 2018; Fernández et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference that is consistent with prior functional hypotheses.

claim: The origin of bipedalism cannot be explained as an initial shift toward terrestriality from a more exclusively arboreal ancestor.
source: These analyses show that the origin of bipedalism cannot be explained as an initial shift toward terrestriality from a more exclusively arboreal ancestor (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the evolutionary modeling analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Early hominins, including Ardipithecus ramidus, evolved from an ancestor with an African ape-like foot adapted to terrestrial plantigrade quadrupedalism.
source: Instead, early hominins, including Ar. ramidus, evolved from an ancestor with an African ape-like foot adapted to terrestrial plantigrade quadrupedalism (Morton, 1922; Wasburn, 1967; Gebo, 1992; Gebo, 1996).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the evolutionary modeling and ancestral state estimation.

claim: Evidence for terrestrial plantigrade quadrupedalism in the Homo-Pan LCA raises the question of whether or not purported knuckle-walking traits in hominines might be homologies rather than homoplasies.
source: Evidence for terrestrial plantigrade quadrupedalism in the Homo-Pan LCA raises the question of whether or not purported knuckle-walking traits in hominines might be homologies (Richmond et al., 2001; Gebo, 1996; Begun, 2004; Inouye and Shea, 2004) rather than homoplasies (Dainton and Macho, 1999; Dainton, 2001; White et al., 2015; Lovejoy et al., 2009b; Kivell and Schmitt, 2009).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of the study's findings for the knuckle-walking debate.

claim: The knuckle-walking hand posture of African apes is hypothesized to be a secondary adaptation to terrestriality in taxa that retain long hands in association with below-branch forelimb suspension.
source: The knuckle-walking hand posture of African apes is hypothesized to be a secondary adaptation to terrestriality in taxa that retain long hands in association with below-branch forelimb suspension (Tuttle, 1969).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature.

claim: There is no special relationship between plantigrade foot postures and knuckle-walking hand postures.
source: However, there is no special relationship between plantigrade foot postures and knuckle-walking hand postures (e.g., plantigrade non-primate mammals do not have a knuckle-walking hand posture).
evidence: This is a comparative observation about the independence of foot and hand postures.

claim: Whether or not modern humans evolved from a knuckle-walking ancestor relies on the analysis of the hand and wrist.
source: Whether or not modern humans evolved from a knuckle-walking ancestor relies on the analysis of the hand and wrist (Tuttle, 1969; Gebo, 1996; Dainton, 2001; Begun, 2004; Inouye and Shea, 2004; Dainton and Macho, 1999; Kivell and Schmitt, 2009; Almécija et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of foot-based analyses for addressing the knuckle-walking question.

claim: The hand of Ardipithecus ramidus was argued not to display traits associated with forelimb suspension in extant taxa or show evidence of a knuckle-walking ancestry.
source: The hand of Ar. ramidus was argued not to display traits associated with forelimb suspension in extant taxa or show evidence of a knuckle-walking ancestry (White et al., 2015; Lovejoy et al., 2009b; Almécija et al., 2015), but many of those observations have not yet been independently validated.
evidence: This is a claim from prior literature that is noted as not yet independently validated.

claim: Many observations about the Ardipithecus ramidus hand have not yet been independently validated.
source: The hand of Ar. ramidus was argued not to display traits associated with forelimb suspension in extant taxa or show evidence of a knuckle-walking ancestry (White et al., 2015; Lovejoy et al., 2009b; Almécija et al., 2015), but many of those observations have not yet been independently validated.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding the Ardipithecus ramidus hand.

claim: The terrestrial specializations of the hominine foot are likely to be homologous because they are present in Ardipithecus ramidus and they are consistent with model-based ancestral estimations.
source: The terrestrial specializations of the hominine foot are likely to be homologous because they are present in Ar. ramidus and they are consistent with model-based ancestral estimations.
evidence: This is an inference from the presence of terrestrial foot traits in Ardipithecus ramidus and the ancestral state estimations.

claim: The terrestrial specializations of the hominine foot carry a similar set of implications for the origin of bipedalism regardless of the terrestrial hand posture of the Homo-Pan LCA.
source: Critically, they carry a similar set of implications for the origin of bipedalism regardless of the terrestrial hand posture of the Homo-Pan LCA.
evidence: This is a statement about the robustness of the study's conclusions to uncertainty about hand posture.

claim: This study provides evidence that modern humans evolved from an ancestor with an African ape-like foot associated with terrestrial plantigrady and vertical climbing.
source: This study provides evidence that modern humans evolved from an ancestor with an African ape-like foot associated with terrestrial plantigrady and vertical climbing.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Hominin upright walking likely emerged in the context of semi-terrestrial quadrupedalism.
source: Hominin upright walking therefore likely emerged in the context of semi-terrestrial quadrupedalism.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's findings about the ancestral condition.

claim: Explaining the adaptive origin of hominin bipedalism will continue to be a challenging endeavor.
source: Explaining the adaptive origin of hominin bipedalism (i.e., 'why' bipedalism evolved) will continue to be a challenging endeavor (Smith and Wood, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the difficulty of testing adaptive hypotheses.

claim: The comparative and fossil material provides evidence for patterns of evolution and strongly suggests that hypotheses of a non-African ape-like morphology for the foot of the Homo-Pan LCA are inconsistent with the results from this study.
source: However, the comparative and fossil material provides evidence for patterns of evolution (i.e., 'how' bipedalism evolved) and strongly suggests that hypotheses of a non-African ape-like morphology for the foot of the Homo-Pan LCA (Lovejoy et al., 2009a; White et al., 2015; Lovejoy et al., 2009b) are inconsistent with the results from this study.
evidence: This is a conclusion that contradicts prior hypotheses based on the study's results.

claim: The Ardipithecus ramidus ARA-VP-6/500 partial skeleton is remarkable for its preservation of multiple areas of anatomy.
source: The Ar. ramidus ARA-VP-6/500 partial skeleton is remarkable for its preservation of multiple areas of anatomy (Lovejoy et al., 2009a; White et al., 2009; White et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the quality of the fossil specimen.

claim: This study provides evidence that intrinsic foot proportions reflect locomotor diversity among anthropoid primates.
source: This study provides evidence that intrinsic foot proportions reflect locomotor diversity among anthropoid primates, but it will be important to consider other regions in future comparative studies.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's analyses.

claim: The hypothesis that hominins evolved from a semi-terrestrial quadrupedal ancestor could be tested with detailed quantitative analyses of other aspects of Ardipithecus ramidus postcranial morphology.
source: The hypothesis that hominins evolved from a semi-terrestrial quadrupedal ancestor could be tested with detailed quantitative analyses of other aspects of Ar. ramidus postcranial morphology.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: The extant sample is composed of 385 individuals representing 45 taxa.
source: The extant sample is composed 385 individuals representing 45 taxa: Homo sapiens, Ardipithecus ramidus, Pan troglodytes, Pan paniscus, Gorilla beringei beringei, Gorilla beringei graueri, Gorilla gorilla, Pongo pygmaeus, Pongo abelii, Hylobates lar, Hylobates muelleri, Hylobates klossii, Hylobates agilis, Hoolock hoolock, Symphalangus syndactylus, Macaca fascicularis, Macaca nemestrina, Papio anubis, Papio hamadryas, Theropithecus gelada, Lophocebus albigena, Mandrillus sphinx, Mandrillus leucophaeus, Cercocebus spp., Erythrocebus patas, Chlorocebus aethiops, Cercopithecus mitis, Miopithecus talapoin, Nasalis larvatus, Colobus polykomos, Trachypithecus cristatus, Semnopithecus entellus, Ateles geoffroyi, Ateles fusciceps, Ateles paniscus, Ateles belzebuth, Alouatta palliata, Alouatta seniculus, Lagothrix lagotricha, Cebus spp., Saimiri spp., Aotus spp., Pithecia spp., Chiropotes spp., and Callicebus donicophilus.
evidence: This is a description of the sample used in the study.

claim: Measurements of Ardipithecus ramidus were initially taken on casts at the University of California, Berkeley.
source: Measurements of Ardipithecus ramidus (ARA-VP-6/500) were initially taken on casts at the University of California, Berkeley.
evidence: This is a description of the data collection methods.

claim: Observations were made on the original Ardipithecus ramidus fossils at the National Museum of Ethiopia and measurements confirmed by T. White.
source: Observations were then made on the original fossils at the National Museum of Ethiopia (NME) and measurements confirmed by T. White.
evidence: This is a description of the data collection and validation methods.

claim: Six measurements were taken on the foot of each individual using Mitutoyo digital calipers.
source: Six measurements were taken on the foot of each individual using Mitutoyo digital calipers: maximum talar articular length, talar trochlea length, cuboid length, first metatarsal (MT1) length, fifth metatarsal length (MT5), and fourth proximal phalanx (PP4) length.
evidence: This is a description of the data collection methods.

claim: The fossil Ardipithecus ramidus foot is missing most of its metatarsal head and its length was estimated by Lovejoy et al. using a combination of anatomical and statistical estimation.
source: The fossil is missing most of its metatarsal head and its length was estimated by Lovejoy et al. (2009a) using a combination of anatomical and statistical estimation.
evidence: This is a description of how missing data was handled in prior work.

claim: Increasing the length of the first metatarsal should increase the moment arm of the intrinsic adductor musculature across a range of hallucal abduction angles, and therefore should increase the hallucal adduction force during grasping in non-human primates.
source: Increasing the length of the first metatarsal should increase the moment arm of the intrinsic adductor musculature such as the m. adductor hallucis across a range of hallucal abduction angles, and therefore should increase the hallucal adduction force during grasping in non-human primates (Cartmill, 1979).
evidence: This is a biomechanical hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: Increasing hallucal metatarsal and non-hallucal phalangeal lengths contributes to increasing the span of the pedal grasp in taxa with a mobile hallux, which helps to maintain a friction grip in pedal grasping.
source: Increasing hallucal metatarsal and non-hallucal phalangeal lengths also contributes to increasing the span of the pedal grasp in taxa with a mobile hallux, which also helps to maintain a friction grip in pedal grasping (Cartmill, 1979).
evidence: This is a biomechanical hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: Previous studies have modeled the foot skeleton as a second-class lever, where the fulcrum is at the metatarsophalangeal joints, the load passes through the talocrural joint at the rearfoot, and the force is produced by the plantarflexor muscles.
source: Previous studies have modeled the foot skeleton as a second-class lever, where the fulcrum is at the metatarsophalangeal joints, the load passes through the talocrural joint at the rearfoot, and the force is produced by the plantarflexor muscles.
evidence: This is a description of a biomechanical model from prior literature.

claim: Increasing the effort arm of the foot relative to the load arm increases the mechanical advantage of the foot skeleton as a lever.
source: Increasing the effort arm of the foot relative to the load arm increases the mechanical advantage of the foot skeleton as a lever (Schultz, 1963a; Schultz, 1963b; Strasser, 1992).
evidence: This is a biomechanical principle supported by citations.

claim: Increasing the load arm increases the range of motion for a given amount of plantarflexor contraction.
source: However, increasing the load arm increases the range of motion for a given amount of plantarflexor contraction (Schultz, 1963a; Schultz, 1963b).
evidence: This is a biomechanical principle supported by citations.

claim: The length of the effort arm of the Ardipithecus ramidus foot is unknown because its calcaneus is not well preserved.
source: The length of the effort arm of the Ar. ramidus foot is unknown because its calcaneus is not well preserved (Lovejoy et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the fossil material.

claim: Increasing the length of the metatarsals subjects them to greater bending moments during stance phase, and therefore increases the possibility of injury.
source: Increasing the length of the metatarsals subjects them to greater bending moments during stance phase, and therefore increases the possibility of injury, so humans achieve a longer load arm by instead increasing the length of the tarsals.
evidence: This is a biomechanical principle used to explain human foot morphology.

claim: Humans achieve a longer load arm by increasing the length of the tarsals rather than the metatarsals.
source: Increasing the length of the metatarsals subjects them to greater bending moments during stance phase, and therefore increases the possibility of injury, so humans achieve a longer load arm by instead increasing the length of the tarsals.
evidence: This is a comparative observation about human foot morphology.

claim: In a bipedal heel-strike plantigrade foot, the load arm is increased by lengthening the cuboid and other midtarsal elements.
source: As such, in a bipedal heel-strike plantigrade foot, the load arm is increased by lengthening the cuboid and other midtarsal elements.
evidence: This is a biomechanical principle about human foot morphology.

claim: In quadrupedal semiplantigrade or digitigrade primates, and other terrestrial cursorial mammals, the load arm is lengthened by increasing the length of the metatarsals.
source: In contrast, in quadrupedal semiplantigrade or digitigrade primates, and indeed other terrestrial cursorial mammals (Taylor, 1976), the load arm is lengthened by increasing the length of the metatarsals.
evidence: This is a comparative biomechanical principle supported by citation.

claim: Foot proportions may be a correlate of foot postures (plantigrady and digitigrady or semiplantigrady).
source: One implication of these differing anatomical arrangements (e.g., increasing metatarsal versus tarsal lengths), is that foot proportions may also be a correlate of foot postures (plantigrady and digitigrady or semiplantigrady), which is one of the hypotheses tested by this study using evolutionary modeling.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: Each measurement was divided by the geometric mean of all six measurements per individual to correct for differences in scale among species.
source: To correct for differences in scale among species, each measurement was divided by the geometric mean of all six measurements per individual (Jungers et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a description of the data standardization method.

claim: Ardipithecus ramidus was added to a molecular phylogenetic tree as a stem hominin with a branch length of 1.4 million years in accordance with first and last appearance data for the genus.
source: Ardipithecus ramidus was added to a molecular phylogenetic tree from 10 k trees (Arnold et al., 2010) as a stem hominin (Strait and Grine, 2004; White et al., 2009; Dembo et al., 2015) with a branch length of 1.4 million years in accordance with first and last appearance data for the genus (5.8–4.4 Ma (Haile-Selassie, 2001; WoldeGabriel et al., 2001)) using Mesquite software (Maddison and Maddison, 2017).
evidence: This is a description of how the fossil was incorporated into the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The branch length for Homo sapiens was reduced in order to improve estimation of phenotypic optima in evolutionary analyses.
source: The branch length for Homo sapiens was reduced in order to improve estimation of phenotypic optima in evolutionary analyses (Butler and King, 2004; Ingram and Mahler, 2013).
evidence: This is a description of a methodological choice in the evolutionary modeling.

claim: Ancestral values estimated under constant rate Brownian motion are affected by taxa that are exceptionally phenotypically derived compared to their close relatives because it is assumed that all branches have evolved at the same rate.
source: Ancestral values estimated under constant rate Brownian motion are affected by taxa that are exceptionally phenotypically derived compared to their close relatives because it is assumed that all branches have evolved at the same rate (Elliot and Mooers, 2014).
evidence: This is a methodological consideration supported by citation.

claim: The assumption of a constant evolutionary rate results in an 'averaging effect' of ancestral values.
source: The assumption of a constant evolutionary rate therefore results in an 'averaging effect' of ancestral values (Schluter et al., 1997; Elliot and Mooers, 2014).
evidence: This is a methodological consideration supported by citation.

claim: The stable model was specifically chosen in light of evidence for molecular and morphological evolutionary rate differences in hominoids relative to other anthropoids and in Homo relative to Pan.
source: Since this study is focused on estimating ancestral values for humans, great apes, and hominoids, the stable model (Elliot and Mooers, 2014) was specifically chosen in light of evidence for molecular and morphological evolutionary rate differences in hominoids relative to other anthropoids (Steiper et al., 2004) and in Homo relative to Pan (Weaver and Stringer, 2015).
evidence: This is a justification for the methodological choice supported by citations.

claim: The estimated value for the Homo-Pan LCA is nearest to the African apes and highly distinct from all other taxa.
source: The estimated value for the Homo-Pan LCA is nearest to the African apes and highly distinct from all other taxa (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a result from the ancestral state estimation shown in Figure 4.

claim: The 95% credibility intervals for the PC scores of the node representing the Homo-Pan LCA are relatively narrow and include the mean values for Pan paniscus and Gorilla gorilla.
source: The 95% credibility intervals for the PC scores of the node representing the Homo-Pan LCA are relatively narrow and include the mean values for Pan paniscus and Gorilla gorilla.
evidence: This is a result from the ancestral state estimation analysis.

claim: The estimated ancestral values for both hominids and hominoids are nearest to Alouatta and Lagothrix.
source: The estimated ancestral values for both hominids and hominoids are nearest to Alouatta and Lagothrix, which is consistent with prior suggestions based on the comparative morphology of the foot in extant and fossil taxa (Gebo, 1996; Sarmiento, 1983; Langdon, 1985; Harrison, 1986).
evidence: This is a result from the ancestral state estimation that is consistent with prior hypotheses.
